passage:
July in Cape Town meant rain on the residence windows and heaters that clicked all night. For three weeks the first-year group chat had been doing the same thing to Alejandro: voice notes imitating his accent, a photo of him asleep in the library captioned "the tourist". When he muted the chat, a senior messaged him: "Relax, it's just first-year fun. Everyone gets it."
That evening he knocked on Zanele's door. She was the residence mentor, and she put the kettle on while he scrolled through the messages for her, his voice flat.
"They say it's just fun."
Zanele read for a long while. "This is you being mocked, over and over, in front of eighty people. You're allowed to call it that." She wrote down the dates. "I'm taking this to the residence head tonight, and I'll tell you tomorrow morning what happens next."

qa.q: What did the senior message Alejandro after he muted the chat?
qa.a: "Relax, it's just first-year fun. Everyone gets it."

qa.q: How was Alejandro feeling when he showed Zanele the messages?
qa.a: His flat voice suggests he felt worn down and hurt, and perhaps unsure he had a right to be upset, since he had been told it was only fun.

qa.q: What did Zanele do that helped?
qa.a: Zanele read the messages, named them plainly as repeated mocking, wrote down the dates, and took it to the residence head that same night, promising to update him in the morning.

qa.q: How might the senior who wrote "just fun" see the chat, and what does that miss?
qa.a: The senior probably sees it as ordinary first-year teasing that everyone goes through, which misses that for Alejandro it has been three weeks of being laughed at in front of eighty people.

grounding: A student mocked for weeks in a group chat is told it is just fun, and a mentor names it plainly and acts the same night.

passage:
Kalyani, you asked why I went quiet after the town hall. Okay. So the director's up there with his slides, saying the Pune unit is being "rightsized" and the late nights are "a stretch culture that motivates us". And everyone nods, because those words sound like nothing is happening to anyone.
And I, Sarika, the one who never raises her hand, raised my hand. I said, "Can we say what that means? How many people lose their jobs, and in which teams? And the stretch culture, is that the twelve-hour days on the support desk?"
The room went very still. He said, "Around forty roles. Mostly support." Forty. Once somebody said forty out loud, people started asking about notice periods, about help for the ones leaving. The whole meeting changed. That's why I went quiet after. I was shaking a little, honestly.

qa.q: How many roles did the director say were going?
qa.a: Around forty roles, mostly support.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after asking the question?
qa.a: Sarika felt shaken and nervous after speaking up in a still room, though the question clearly mattered to her.

qa.q: Why was Sarika's question an effective way to respond?
qa.a: Asking how many people, which teams, and what "stretch" means turned soft labels into real people and real hours, and the room started asking about notice periods and help for those leaving.

qa.q: How might the support staff in the room have felt when the number was said?
qa.a: For the support staff, hearing "forty, mostly support" was probably frightening but also clearer, because the soft words had hidden that it was about them.

grounding: An adult hears a layoff called rightsizing and pressure called motivation, and asks what actually happens to whom.

passage:
Garba practice week, Class 4: note for the class file.
At lunch five girls sat on the steps and kept the space closed off with their bags. Parveen came with her tiffin, and Rashmi said, "This place is taken," and moved her bag over the last gap. Parveen ate alone near the water cooler, turning her roti over.
I spoke to Rashmi after lunch. She said, "But everyone was doing it, not only me. Mahi put her bag first." When I asked what Rashmi herself had done, she looked at her shoes. "I moved my bag."
What I did: sat with Parveen for the rest of lunch; phoned Rashmi's mother this evening; tomorrow I am pairing the girls for the garba circle so each one looks after one partner.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do when Parveen came with her tiffin?
qa.a: Rashmi said, "This place is taken," and moved her bag over the last gap.

qa.q: Why did "everyone was doing it" feel like a real excuse to Rashmi?
qa.a: With five girls blocking the steps, Rashmi felt like only a small part of it and so less guilty; when asked about her own action she looked at her shoes, embarrassed.

qa.q: What makes the teacher's next steps useful?
qa.a: The teacher comforted Parveen, phoned Rashmi's mother that evening, and plans to give each girl one partner, so no one can hide inside the group.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen ate alone by the water cooler turning her roti over, so she probably felt left out and hurt, however many girls shared the blame.

grounding: A child who joined in shutting out a classmate says everyone else was doing it, and a teacher turns the question to her own action.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
On the night before Eid, Irfan was stuck at the counter of his uncle's sweet shop, packing boxes of sevaiyan while the queue curled out the door. His phone buzzed. Tushar: "Send that pic of Manav in the mud to the class group. Do it, it's hilarious." Irfan forwarded it between two customers without really looking.
By morning the photo had forty replies. Manav hadn't come online at all.
After the holiday the class teacher called Irfan in. "Why did you post it?"
"Tushar told me to send it, sir. It was his idea. I was busy, I didn't even think."
"Tushar asked. Whose thumb pressed send?"
Irfan opened his mouth and closed it. The teacher had him delete the photo there and then, said Irfan's father would be called that afternoon, and sent for Tushar next.

qa.q: What was Irfan doing when Tushar's message came?
qa.a: He was packing boxes of sevaiyan at the counter of his uncle's sweet shop while the queue curled out the door.

qa.q: Why does "Tushar told me to" feel like a fair defence to Irfan?
qa.a: Irfan feels defensive and probably ashamed; putting the idea on Tushar and the busy shop lets him feel he wasn't really the one who did it.

qa.q: What was wise about the teacher's question?
qa.a: "Whose thumb pressed send?" handed responsibility back to Irfan without shouting, and the teacher followed through by having the photo deleted, calling his father and speaking to Tushar too.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for Manav?
qa.a: Manav didn't come online at all while forty replies piled up, which suggests he felt humiliated and wanted to hide.

grounding: A teenager who forwarded an embarrassing photo says his friend told him to send it, placing the responsibility on someone else.

passage:
I'm Farhan, and I still think about the evening the hostel group turned on Chinmay. He had posted a shaky video of himself singing at the cultural night, and within an hour there were sixty comments, laughing faces, someone's edit with his voice sped up.
I read every one. I typed "guys, enough" and deleted it three times. There were two hundred people in that group. Seniors. Class reps. Surely one of them would say something. Nobody did. I remember thinking, it's not my place, I barely know him.
Then, around midnight, a first-year called Anjali wrote: "He sang in front of everyone, which none of us did. Can we stop?" That was all. The comments slowed, and a few people deleted theirs. I wished it had been me.

qa.q: What did Anjali write around midnight?
qa.a: "He sang in front of everyone, which none of us did. Can we stop?"

qa.q: Why did Farhan keep deleting "guys, enough"?
qa.a: Farhan felt uneasy and unsure; with two hundred people in the group, it seemed someone more senior would speak up, and it felt like it wasn't Farhan's place.

qa.q: What does Anjali's message show about stopping a pile-on?
qa.a: One short, calm message that names something decent about the target and asks the group to stop can shift everyone: the comments slowed and some were deleted.

qa.q: What might that evening have been like for Chinmay?
qa.a: Chinmay had shared a brave performance and then watched sixty mocking comments pile up, so it was likely humiliating and lonely until someone finally spoke up.

grounding: A student watching an online pile-on waits for someone else to speak, until one calm voice breaks the silence.

passage:
At the helmet factory in Faridabad, the Friday shipment was already loaded when Jagdish found hairline cracks in twelve shells from batch 41. He carried one to the production manager's cabin.
"Mark them passed," the manager said, not looking up from his screen. "The client wants the full lot today. My responsibility."
Jagdish stood there a moment, turning the shell in his hands. "I understand the instruction, sir. But my name goes on the quality sheet. If a rider falls in one of these, that's on me too."
He wrote the defect in the log, photographed the cracks, and took the log upstairs to Rehana in compliance. She read it, picked up her phone, and stopped the truck at the gate. "Pull batch 41," she told the loading bay. "Jagdish, thank you. I'll handle the conversation with production."

qa.q: What did Jagdish find in batch 41?
qa.a: Hairline cracks in twelve shells.

qa.q: Why didn't Jagdish feel covered by the manager's "my responsibility"?
qa.a: Jagdish felt uneasy and personally responsible: his name goes on the quality sheet, and he was worried a rider could be hurt, whatever the manager said.

qa.q: Which steps made Jagdish's stand effective?
qa.a: He stayed respectful, recorded the defect in the log with photos, and took it to compliance instead of arguing or quietly obeying, so the proper channel could act.

qa.q: How does Rehana treat Jagdish's report?
qa.a: Rehana takes it seriously at once: she stops the truck at the gate, has batch 41 pulled, thanks Jagdish and takes on the talk with production herself. 👍

grounding: An employee told to pass defective goods accepts the instruction was given but stays accountable for his own actions and reports it through compliance.

passage:
Summer reading camp, Ward 12 library: volunteer's note, Day 6.
Too hot outside, so I paired the children for a board game. When I paired Zainab with Salma from Kasai Gali, Zainab pushed her chair back. "Not with her. Those Kasai Gali kids are dirty. They're like wild dogs." Salma went very still and stared at the board.
I didn't argue in front of everyone. I asked Zainab to help me carry the water jug, and on the way I asked, "What's Salma's favourite game?" She didn't know. "Then find out one thing about her first."
Back at the table, Salma said ludo, and taught Zainab a new rule. They played two rounds. Tomorrow I will mix the street groups for every activity and speak to both families.

qa.q: What did Zainab say when she was paired with Salma?
qa.a: "Not with her. Those Kasai Gali kids are dirty. They're like wild dogs."

qa.q: Why might calling Salma's street "wild" feel right to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab seems wary and a bit superior; if the Kasai Gali children are "wild", pushing away feels fair, and Zainab doesn't have to feel bad about hurting anyone.

qa.q: What did the volunteer do that helped?
qa.a: The volunteer avoided a public scolding, asked Zainab privately about Salma's favourite game, and got the two to learn something real about each other, with mixed groups and family talks planned next.

qa.q: What was that moment like for Salma?
qa.a: Salma went very still and stared at the board, so being called dirty and wild probably felt humiliating and hurtful.

grounding: A child calls children from another street dirty and wild and refuses to play, and a volunteer helps her see one real person.

subtype: Mocking a group as not real people [Actor]
passage:
Gopika, pass me my glasses. You asked what I was like at sixteen. Not so nice, kanna. That Pongal, families from the dam construction set up a camp near our town, and in the school yard we had jokes about them. "Dam donkeys," we called them. "What does a dam donkey eat? Whatever you throw." Your Harsha Thatha told those jokes loudest and got the biggest laughs.
Then, at the Pongal games, a boy from the camp, Velu, fell into the temple tank reaching for the pot. I was standing nearest. I pulled him out, and he coughed and said, "Thank you, anna," in a voice just like my little brother's.
After that I couldn't find any donkey in him. I only saw Velu, shivering, with a scraped knee. The jokes turned sour in my mouth.

qa.q: What did young Harsha and his classmates call the families from the dam camp?
qa.a: "Dam donkeys."

qa.q: Why did telling the jokes feel fine to young Harsha at first?
qa.a: Young Harsha felt proud of the big laughs, and since the camp families were only "donkeys" in the jokes, there seemed to be nothing cruel to feel guilty about.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Harsha's story?
qa.a: Pulling Velu out of the tank and hearing "Thank you, anna" gave the group a real face; after that Harsha saw a shivering boy, not a joke, and stopped enjoying them.

qa.q: How might the camp children have felt hearing those jokes in the school yard?
qa.a: They were probably hurt and ashamed, treated as a laughing-stock in a new town instead of as children with names like Velu.

grounding: An elder recalls repeating jokes that called an outsider group animals, until one boy's face made the cruelty impossible to keep up.

passage:
During the wheat harvest in Moga, the polytechnic office was half-staffed, and the clerk never looked up. "Roll 117, form incomplete. You people always come late." Nitin had come from Darbhanga two months ago, and by now he answered to 117 faster than to his own name. In the workshop the instructor pointed at him with a spanner: "You, the outsider at the back." On the bus a man grumbled about "these fellows" taking all the seats.
That evening Nitin sat on the hostel roof, scrolling to his mother's number without calling.
Gurpreet climbed up with two glasses of lassi from the Baisakhi stall. "Nitin! You missed the bhangra. My chachi keeps asking where the boy who fixed her pump went."
Nitin laughed for the first time that day. He called his mother after that, and on Sunday he went to the fair in Gurpreet's village.

qa.q: What did the clerk call Nitin?
qa.a: "Roll 117", telling him the form was incomplete.

qa.q: What does Nitin scrolling to his mother's number without calling suggest?
qa.a: Nitin seems lonely and low, worn down by a day of being treated as a number and a burden, perhaps not wanting to worry his mother.

qa.q: What helped Nitin, and what else could help?
qa.a: Gurpreet using his name and pulling him into family and the fair helped; keeping close to people like his mother and Gurpreet, and raising the office's treatment with the hostel warden, could help more.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Nitin?
qa.a: To Gurpreet, Nitin is a person with a name and a place, the one who fixed the chachi's pump and was missed at the bhangra. 😊

grounding: A migrant student is called a roll number and an outsider, and staying close to someone who uses his name eases the pain.

passage:
Chaitanya, you said at lunch that the cleaning contractors are "all lazy". Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, new in this same office, and your Kavitha-ma'am was not much wiser.
Delivery riders used to wait in our lobby during the rains, and people complained. "They smell, they're rude, they're all the same." Something about "all the same" bothered me. So I asked Mr Rao, who complained loudest, "Which one? Tell me one name." He couldn't.
Next time it rained, I asked the rider by the door his name. Suresh. He was studying accounts at night college, and he waited inside because his phone had to stay dry for the orders. After that, "they" got harder for all of us to say.
So, Chaitanya. Which cleaner? What name?

qa.q: Why did Suresh wait inside the lobby?
qa.a: Because his phone had to stay dry for the orders.

qa.q: Why did "all the same" bother young Kavitha?
qa.a: Young Kavitha felt uneasy with the sweeping contempt; since nobody could name even one rider, it seemed hollow, and she grew curious about the actual people.

qa.q: Which choice in the story brought back empathy, and why?
qa.a: Asking for one name and then asking the rider himself; hearing about Suresh's night college and his reason for waiting turned a faceless group into a person, which made contempt harder.

qa.q: How might Suresh have experienced the lobby before anyone asked his name?
qa.a: Suresh was probably used to being treated as part of a rude, smelly crowd while people complained around him, so being asked his name may have felt like being seen at last.

grounding: An elder recalls hearing a group described with contempt and asking for one person's name and story, which brought back empathy.
